554.title: The lowest seat (Luke 14:1–14)
554.hook: don't take the top place; invite those who can't repay you
554.howItsDone: Some churches and Christian groups run community meals and soup kitchens open to anyone, and some Christians make a habit of inviting people who are often left out to their own tables, especially at holidays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hen with her wings open over Jerusalem, and Herod the fox. Your line was under her wings.

A wedding reception, and no seating plan. Near the head table, a few empty chairs. At the back, by the kitchen door, a table where nobody seems to know anybody. Where do you sit? Luke says Jesus is at a Sabbath dinner in the house of one of the chief Pharisees, watching the guests come in. He marks how they choose the chief rooms, the best places at the table. And then, being Jesus, he says so.

His advice starts out sounding like good manners. Don't grab the top place; someone more honored might arrive, the host will ask you to move, and you'll walk the whole room to the bottom with everyone watching. Instead, in the King James Bible: "go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher." Room there means place, a seat at the table. This wasn't new wisdom. The book of Proverbs says nearly the same: don't push yourself forward before the king, because it's better to be told come up here than to be put lower. Jesus is drawing on his own people's old wisdom. Then he lifts it into something bigger: "For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted." That's not seating strategy anymore. In Jesus' telling, it's how God turns things over. Then he turns to the host, and it gets more uncomfortable. When you give a dinner, don't just invite friends, family and rich neighbors, who'll invite you back. "But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee." He asks for a guest list of people who can't pay you back. The repayment, he says, comes later, at the resurrection of the just. Lowest seat for the guest. Open door for the host. Both are about letting go of the score.

Run through the people you usually share meals or time with, and notice how many return the favor; that's normal and good. Then widen the circle to someone who rarely gets invited anywhere, an older neighbor living alone, a new coworker, someone in a hard time with nothing to offer back, and picture setting a place for them at your table. If you pray, ask for open doors.
Proverbs. The book Jesus echoes when he tells a dinner guest to take the lowest seat and let the host call him up higher, rather than pushing to the front.
Your line: friend, go up higher. The host does the calling up, not the guest. That's day five hundred fifty-four.

a short story Jesus told to teach

555.title: Excuses (Luke 14:15–24)
555.hook: a field, oxen, a marriage: good reasons to miss the feast
555.howItsDone: Many Christians hear this story as an invitation to worship and to the Lord's Supper, and some churches echo the servant's words when they invite people to the table at communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lowest seat, old wisdom from Proverbs, and your line: friend, go up higher.

Sorry, can't make it tonight, something's come up. Most of us have sent that message, and usually the reason is real enough: work ran late, the kids are tired, we need a night in. Back at the same dinner table, a guest says something pious and safe: "Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God." A lovely thought about a feast someday. Jesus answers with a story about a feast right now, and the very human art of the polite excuse.

A man prepares a great supper and invites many. In that world, guests were often invited ahead of time, then a servant came to fetch them when the meal was ready. That's this moment. The servant goes out with the message, in the King James Bible: "Come; for all things are now ready." And then: "they all with one consent began to make excuse." All of them. And they're good excuses. "I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused." The second: "I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to prove them." Ten oxen, a big purchase; he wants to test them. The third doesn't even ask to be excused: "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come." Land, business, family. Not one of them is a bad thing. Some commentators point out that nobody buys a field without seeing it, or oxen without trying them, so the excuses may be thinner than they sound. Either way, the host is left with a feast and an empty hall. He's angry, and then he does something astonishing. Go out quickly, he tells the servant, into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind. When there's still room, go further, to the highways and hedges. The feast happens anyway. The story isn't against fields, oxen or marriages. It's about good things becoming the reason we miss the best thing. And in the story the invitation never closes: the servant keeps going out until the house is full.
screen: then, large: `THEY ALL WITH ONE CONSENT BEGAN TO MAKE EXCUSE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few weeks and what you said no to: a call from an old friend, a community event, a quiet time of prayer you kept postponing, a walk someone suggested. Without judging yourself, notice which noes were honest rest and which were a field and five oxen. If you pray, listen for the words: come, for all is ready.
Excuses. A field, five yoke of oxen and a new marriage: good reasons, given all at once, to miss a feast that was already ready.
Your line: come, for all is ready. Honest rest isn't an excuse. Day five hundred fifty-five, done.

556.title: Count the cost (Luke 14:25–35)
556.hook: a builder counts the cost before starting a tower
556.howItsDone: Some churches ask adults to prepare over weeks or months before baptism, confirmation or membership, and religious orders give long periods of testing before final vows, so people can count the cost first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, excuses: a field, five yoke of oxen, a new marriage, and a feast that filled anyway. Your line was come, for all is ready.

Plenty of towns have one: a building started and never finished. Concrete pillars with rusting rods sticking out the top, a fence around it, weeds growing through the foundation. Locals give it a nickname. Drive past, and the thought comes on its own: somebody ran out of money. Jesus uses that same picture at a moment you might not expect, when great crowds are following him down the road.

Luke says great multitudes went with him, and he turned and spoke to them, not to thank the crowd but to slow it down. First a hard saying: whoever comes to him and does not hate father and mother, even their own life, cannot be his disciple. It sounds shocking, and it should be heard carefully. In the Bible's own way of speaking, hate can mean love less, put second. Genesis says Leah was hated, when the story has just said Jacob loved Rachel more. Matthew gives the same saying plainly: "He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." Read that way, Jesus isn't asking anyone to despise their family; he's saying nothing can come before him. Then the picture: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?" Otherwise you lay the foundation, can't finish, and everyone who sees it begins to mock you: "This man began to build, and was not able to finish." Then a king with ten thousand soldiers facing one with twenty thousand: he sits down first, and counts. Notice the word sits, twice. Discipleship here isn't a rush of feeling at the back of a big crowd. It's a decision made sitting down, with the numbers in front of you. And Jesus doesn't hide the total. Luke ends the passage plainly: whoever does not forsake all that he has cannot be his disciple.
screen: `HATE: A BIBLE WAY TO SAY LOVE LESS.`
then, large: `THIS MAN BEGAN TO BUILD, AND WAS NOT ABLE TO FINISH.`

segments.voice: Sit down like the builder and choose one thing you've said yes to, or are about to: a job, a relationship, a promise to volunteer, a faith practice like this one. Count it honestly, item by item, in time, money, energy and what you'll give up, without letting yourself off with a vague answer. Then ask: can I finish this tower?
Genesis. The book where love held second is called hate, the Hebrew way of speaking behind Jesus's hard saying that whoever will not count this cost cannot be his disciple.
Your line: can I finish this tower? The builder sits down before he builds. See you tomorrow.

557.title: This man receives sinners (Luke 15:1–10)
557.hook: grumbling leads to three stories of lost things found
557.howItsDone: Christians read Luke 15 often, especially in Lent, and many churches mark returns with celebration: welcoming people back to communion, to membership, or into recovery communities that meet in church halls.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Genesis, a hard saying heard carefully, and a half-built tower. Your line was can I finish this tower?

A sneer, overheard at the edge of a crowd. That's how Luke chapter fifteen begins. The chapter holds a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son, and it's easy to keep the stories and forget why Jesus told them. They weren't bedtime stories. They were his answer to a complaint, and the complaint itself, meant as an insult, says something true about him.
screen: `A SNEER AT THE EDGE OF A CROWD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them." Publicans were tax collectors, and Luke sets them right beside the word sinners. Sharing a table, in that world, meant accepting someone. So the worry was serious: what does it say about a teacher, about God, if he eats with these people? The Greek word for murmured is a grumbling, muttering word. Some readers hear in it the same word family the old Greek version of Exodus uses when Israel grumbled in the wilderness. Jesus doesn't argue. He tells three stories, and the stakes keep rising. A shepherd loses one sheep out of a hundred. A woman loses one coin out of ten. Tomorrow, a father loses one son out of two. One percent, ten percent, half. And each of the first two ends not with the finding, but with a party. The shepherd calls his friends and neighbors: "Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost." The woman does the same: "Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost." Then Jesus says it straight: "there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth." Here's the twist. The grumblers aren't the villains. They're being invited. Every story ends with someone saying come and celebrate with me. When the lost come home, will you come to the party? This man receives sinners. It was meant as an accusation. Luke keeps it as a description.
screen: `ONE IN A HUNDRED, ONE IN TEN.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who has come back, to health, to sobriety, to the family table, to faith, to talking with you after a long silence, maybe in a way nobody marked. Picture them clearly, notice if any part of you is still grumbling and let it be there, then try for a moment to feel the shepherd's joy instead. If you pray, give thanks for their return.
Publicans. Tax collectors who drew near to hear Jesus, and whose company with him made the Pharisees mutter that this man receives sinners.
Your line: joy in heaven. The finding isn't the end; the party is. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

558.title: The younger son (Luke 15:11–24)
558.hook: he came to himself, rehearsed a speech, and his father interrupted it with a hug
558.carry: while he was still far off
558.howItsDone: Christians read this story often, especially in Lent; Catholics and Orthodox Christians often connect it with confession, and many churches use it to welcome people who are returning after years away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, publicans welcomed, and a lost sheep and a lost coin that ended in parties. Your line was joy in heaven.

Have you ever rehearsed an apology? In the car, in the shower, at three in the morning. You polish every line and lower your expectations so you won't be disappointed. Today's story has a young man doing exactly that, on a long walk home. People call it the prodigal son, though Luke never gives it a title. Jesus just begins: a certain man had two sons. Today, the younger one.

The younger son asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father is alive. Some commentators say that in that world it was close to saying I wish you were dead. The father divides it anyway. The son goes to a far country and wastes it all. Then famine. He ends up feeding pigs, animals his own people's law counted unclean, and in the King James Bible, "he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him." As low as he can go. Then: "when he came to himself." He works out a speech: "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants." Not a son again, just a paid worker. Then the line that turns the story: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Some readers think he'd been watching the road. And he ran; some commentators note that grown men of standing didn't run in public. The son starts the speech, and before he gets to make me a hired servant, the father interrupts, calling to the servants: "Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet." Robe, ring and shoes: you don't put those on a worker. You put them on a son. And the father says why: "this my son was dead, and is alive again."
screen: `HE RAN, WHILE THE SON WAS FAR OFF.`
then, large: `THIS MY SON WAS DEAD, AND IS ALIVE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Think of somewhere you've drifted from, a person, a promise, a practice, a faith, and notice the speech you've been rehearsing for going back: the explanations, the bargaining, the lowered expectations. Then picture the father on the road, already running before you've said a word, and let the speech go quiet. If you pray, simply turn toward God without the speech; if you don't, let yourself be welcomed, in your imagination, before you've earned it.
Splanchna, the Greek word for the inner organs, where compassion is felt — what moved the father to run to his younger son, met on the road before he could finish his speech.
Your line: while he was still far off. The father ran first. Day five hundred fifty-eight, done.

559.title: The older brother (Luke 15:25–32)
559.hook: the faithful son won't come to the party; the story ends with the father pleading
559.howItsDone: Christians often reflect on both brothers when reading this parable in Lent, and some preachers point to the open ending as a question each listener answers in their own life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, splanchna: the father's compassion, running to meet his younger son while he was still far off.

Robe, ring, the fatted calf. A fine place to roll the credits. But the story began with a certain man who had two sons. While the party starts, the older one is still out in the field, working, as he has for years. He comes near the house and hears music. Dancing. He calls a servant over and asks what on earth is going on.
screen: `A FINE PLACE TO ROLL THE CREDITS.`

segments.voice: Your brother is home, the servant says, and your father has killed the fatted calf. In the King James Bible: "And he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came out his father, and intreated him." The father went out to the younger son on the road. Now he goes out again, to the older one in the yard, leaving his own party to plead. And the older son lets it all out: "Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends." Not even a young goat. The word for serve is the word for working as a slave. He's been home all along, living like a hired hand. And he names his brother: this thy son. Not my brother. The father answers gently, with a tender word, teknon, child: "Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine." Everything was already his. He never had to earn it. Then the father hands the brother back to him: "It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found." Thy brother. And the story stops. We never find out if he goes in. Jesus leaves the door open and the music playing. He was talking to people grumbling that he ate with sinners, and some readers hear them in the older brother. Others hear anyone who has been faithful a long time and quietly started keeping score.
screen: then, large: `SON, THOU ART EVER WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Think of a celebration you'd rather skip, because someone is being welcomed who, in your view, hasn't earned it: a colleague's promotion, a sibling's second chance. Notice the old scorecard come out, then hear the father's words to his older son: all that I have is thine. If you pray, hold those words a while; if not, imagine walking in through the door, toward the music.

Your line: all I have is yours. Everything was already his, without earning it. See you tomorrow.

560.title: The shrewd manager (Luke 16:1–13)
560.hook: a puzzling story: use money to make friends; you can't serve two masters
560.howItsDone: Christians use the language of stewardship for money, time and the earth, as things held in trust; many churches teach regular giving, and some Christians keep budgets that set aside money for hospitality and helping others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teknon: the older brother outside the party, and a father who came out to plead. Your line was all I have is yours.

It may be the most puzzling story Jesus tells. A dishonest employee gets praised. Money gets called unrighteous, then used to make friends. Even Luke seems to feel the strain: after the story come four or five different morals, one after another. And a clue links it to the prodigal son. The younger son wasted his father's goods. This manager is accused of wasting his master's goods. Same Greek word. Two stories about what we do with what isn't really ours.

A rich man's manager is caught and told to hand in the books. He panics, and in the King James Bible talks to himself: "What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed." Then an idea. He calls in his master's debtors one by one. How much do you owe? A hundred measures of oil. Quick, write fifty. And you? A hundred measures of wheat. Write eighty. When he's out of a job, they'll owe him a favor. And the punchline: "the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely." Not for honesty. For being shrewd: seeing the crisis coming and acting fast. Scholars genuinely disagree about the details. Some think he cut out his own commission; others, the master's interest; others that he was simply dishonest to the end. The lesson Jesus draws is clear: use the money of this world, mammon, to make friends, because people last and money doesn't. Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth, and Jesus treats it almost like a rival god. Then today's line: "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much." Small things train big things. And the warning: "Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Money makes a fine servant and a terrible master. Look back at the week: Proverbs, a feast refused with excuses, a tower that needs counting, a grumble that started three stories, a son far off, another at the door, and now a manager who saw clearly that his time was short.
